input.question: Diploid vs Haploid cells
input.ground_truth: Cells start as diploid (two copies of each chromosome). They replicate their DNA in S-phase and become tetraploid (4 copies of each chromosome). After mitosis that number is divided by two so each daughter cell is diploid (two copies). In meiosis another division reduces the ploidy so you get four haploid (one copy) gametes. This is in us and many other organisms. The model organism [*Xenopus laevis*](_URL_0_) is tetraploid (four copies of each chromosome). Some plants have [very high ploidy](_URL_1_).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Diploid vs Haploid cells

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big box of crayons. That big box with all the crayons inside is like a **diploid cell**. It has two copies of every color crayon—one from your mom and one from your dad.

Now, imagine you take just one crayon out of the box. That single crayon is like a **haploid cell**. It only has one color, not a pair.

So, diploid cells have **pairs** of everything (like two of each crayon), and haploid cells have just **one** of each thing.

That’s the difference between diploid and haploid cells!
